note: Bundled field guide for TerraLens. General temperate-region naturalist knowledge; not an identification authority. Server-side Tiger Data can extend this set.

entries.habitat: Parkland, hedgerows, old woodland across temperate Europe.
entries.ecology: Oaks can live for centuries and support hundreds of insect species; jays bury acorns and often plant the next generation of oaks by forgetting a few.
safeFacts: Acorns are not edible raw for people.
Oak processionary moth caterpillars have irritating hairs — look, don't touch.

entries.habitat: Heathland, woodland edges and open ground; a pioneer tree on bare soil.
entries.ecology: One of the first trees to colonise cleared ground. Its light seeds travel far on the wind, and its bark peels in papery horizontal strips.
safeFacts: Birch pollen is a common allergen in spring.

entries.habitat: Damp woodland, ditches and lakesides.
entries.ecology: Its early catkins are one of the first big pollen sources for bees waking from winter. Willows root readily from broken branches.
safeFacts: Willow bark contains salicin, a relative of aspirin — do not self-medicate from wild trees.

entries.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub and field edges — the classic hedge plant.
entries.ecology: Blossom feeds insects in May and the autumn haws feed thrushes and redwings through winter. Old hawthorns often host lichens and nesting birds.
safeFacts: The thorns are sharp enough to scratch — long sleeves help in tight hedges.

entries.habitat: Parks, avenues and large gardens.
entries.ecology: Introduced from the Balkans but planted widely. Its 'candles' of flowers appear in May, followed by conkers in spiky cases each autumn.
safeFacts: Conkers are mildly toxic — not for eating.

entries.habitat: Gardens, hedgerows and woodland undergrowth.
entries.ecology: Robins follow digging animals and gardeners to snap up exposed worms — the origin of their famously bold behaviour. Both sexes look alike and hold winter territories with song.

entries.habitat: Woodland, gardens and parks; nests in tree holes and nest boxes.
entries.ecology: Famous for pecking the foil tops off milk bottles for cream — a learned habit spread between birds. A single brood can eat thousands of caterpillars.

entries.habitat: Dense undergrowth, log piles, stone walls, gardens.
entries.ecology: Gram for gram one of the loudest singers in Europe. In cold snaps wrens roost together in huddles to share warmth.
entries.region: Europe and North America (as winter wren group)

entries.habitat: Ponds, rivers, canals — almost any water in town or country.
entries.ecology: During summer moult males go dull brown and briefly cannot fly. Ducklings leave the nest within a day and can swim almost immediately.
safeFacts: Bread harms waterfowl — offer oats, seeds or leave them be.

entries.habitat: Fields, coasts, parks and city rooftops.
entries.ecology: Crows solve puzzles and even use sticks as tools in experiments. They cache food and remember who was watching when they hid it.

entries.habitat: Farmland, towns, parks and scrub.
entries.ecology: One of the few non-mammals to pass the mirror test — magpies react to a mark they only see in a reflection. Their domed nests with side entrances are unlike most open bird nests.

entries.habitat: Rough grassland, motorway verges, church towers and cliffs.
entries.ecology: Kestrels hover into the wind scanning for voles, dropping in a controlled dive. They can see ultraviolet, which helps them follow vole urine trails.

entries.habitat: Gaps under roof tiles and in old walls; hawks insects high over towns.
entries.ecology: After fledging, a young swift may stay airborne for almost ten months — eating, sleeping and even mating in flight. They arrive in May and leave in August.
seasonality: screaming party flights on warm evenings
safeFacts: A grounded swift needs urgent specialist help — it cannot take off from the ground.

entries.habitat: Woodland, farmland, parks and gardens.
entries.ecology: Wood pigeons can swallow surprising-sized acorns and berries whole. Their lazy 'coo-COO-coo, coo' rhythm is one of the most recognisable sounds of a British summer.

entries.habitat: Broadleaf and mixed woodland, parks with mature trees.
entries.ecology: Drumming is a territorial signal, not feeding — the bird strikes a resonant dead branch with rapid beats. Its tongue wraps around the skull under the skin, cushioning the impacts.
seasonality: visits feeders for peanuts in winter

entries.habitat: Lawns, verges, cracks in pavement — almost anywhere.
entries.ecology: Each 'petal' is a complete tiny flower, and the seed clock is a precise parachute. Dandelions flower over a long season, feeding pollinators when little else is out.
safeFacts: Edible in salads only when picked from clean ground away from dogs and spraying.

entries.habitat: Woodland clearings, hedgebanks and acidic soils.
entries.ecology: Foxgloves are biennial: a rosette one year, a towering flower spike the next. The spotted inner petals are landing lights for bumblebees, which are the only insects strong enough to push inside.
safeFacts: All parts of foxglove are toxic — admire, don't pick or ingest, and wash hands after touching.

entries.habitat: Meadows, verges and clover leys.
entries.ecology: Clovers fix nitrogen with root bacteria, enriching the soil around them. Bumblebees with long tongues are their main pollinators.

entries.habitat: Waste ground, hedgerows, riverbanks — soils rich in nutrients.
entries.ecology: The nettle's stinging hairs are tiny glass-like tubes that snap and inject irritants. Red admiral and peacock butterflies lay eggs on nettles, making them vital caterpillar food.
safeFacts: Stings sting — cooling water helps; dock leaves are tradition rather than true remedy.

entries.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges.
entries.ecology: Brambles root wherever their arching tips touch soil, forming impenetrable thickets that shelter birds and small mammals. The blackberries are vital autumn food.
safeFacts: Pick berries above dog height and wash before eating; thorns scratch — check for ticks afterwards.

entries.habitat: Tree trunks, walls, hedgebanks and shade.
entries.ecology: Ivy is not a parasite — it climbs with rootlets and only uses trees for support. Its late-autumn flowers are a lifeline for bees and hoverflies, and the spring berries feed thrushes.
safeFacts: Berries are toxic to people — leave them for the birds.

entries.habitat: Lawns, paths and pasture — thrives where feet and mowers press down.
entries.ecology: Its rosette grows flat, surviving being walked on. The seed heads rattle with the wind and are nicknamed 'fighting cocks' for a children's game of knocking heads off.

entries.habitat: Gardens, meadows and farmland; nests in old mouse holes or under sheds.
entries.ecology: Workers have a buff tail; only queens have the buff tail edged in white. They 'buzz-pollinate' tomatoes and blueberries by vibrating flowers to shake out pollen.
safeFacts: Bumblebees are gentle and rarely sting — stay still and let them pass.

entries.habitat: Gardens, fields and hedgerows wherever aphids gather.
entries.ecology: One ladybird larva can eat hundreds of aphids before pupating. The bright red is a warning: they can bleed bitter fluid from their leg joints when threatened.
entries.region: Europe and Asia (introduced to North America)

entries.habitat: Ponds, ditches and still water; often perches on warm wood.
entries.ecology: Dragonfly young live underwater as ferocious nymphs for a year or more before climbing out to split their skins and fly. Adults hunt midges and flies on warm afternoons.
seasonality: one of the last dragonflies flying into autumn

entries.habitat: Gardens, nettle patches and buddleia bushes.
entries.ecology: When disturbed, a peacock can hiss by rubbing its wings and flash four eyespots to startle birds. Adults hibernate with wings closed looking like dead leaves.

entries.habitat: Under birch, pine and spruce, often in rings.
entries.ecology: The classic storybook toadstool. It partners with tree roots: the fungus trades soil minerals for tree sugars in a mutualism called a mycorrhiza.
safeFacts: Toxic and psychoactive — never eat any wild mushroom identified only from an app or photo.

entries.habitat: Rotting stumps and logs, often in tiers.
entries.ecology: A white-rot fungus that secretes enzymes to break down wood, releasing nutrients back into the soil. The banded patterns are why it is called 'turkey tail'.
safeFacts: Never eat wild fungi identified from an app; turkey tail lookalikes exist.

entries.habitat: Walls, tombstones, rocks and old trees.
entries.ecology: A lichen is not one organism but a partnership of fungus and alga. Crustose lichens grow so slowly they can be decades old — some Arctic ones are thousands of years old.
safeFacts: Lichens are sensitive to pollution — lush lichen usually means cleaner air.

entries.habitat: Anywhere with trees, hedges and birds — strongest near woodland edge.
entries.ecology: At dawn the air is still and dim, so low-frequency song travels well. Robins and blackbirds start earliest, then a rolling sequence as each species joins in.
safeFacts: Best heard by simply standing still — recording playback can disturb nesting birds.

entries.habitat: High in the sky, often ahead of a change in weather.
entries.ecology: Rows of small rounded clouds form where moist air ripples in stable layers. Sailors read them as a sign the weather is about to turn within a day.

entries.habitat: Cliffs, quarries, dry valleys and karst landscapes.
entries.ecology: Most limestone is the compressed remains of sea creatures — a rock made of biology. Fossils of shells and corals are often visible with the naked eye.
safeFacts: Old quarries and cliff edges are unstable — keep back from faces and loose blocks.

entries.habitat: Woodland edges, farmland and scrub — often at dawn and dusk.
entries.ecology: Roe deer delay implanting the embryo so young are born when food is best. When alarmed they bark, a surprisingly harsh sound for a delicate-looking animal.
safeFacts: Give them space; a cornered deer can be dangerous, and does will defend hidden fawns.

entries.habitat: Woodland and parks; introduced and now widespread.
entries.ecology: Grey squirrels scatter-hoard thousands of nuts each autumn, remembering the locations better than almost any other small mammal. Forgotten caches plant trees.
safeFacts: Do not hand-feed — bites are serious and processed human food harms them.

entries.habitat: Gardens, hedgerows and parks with plenty of cover.
entries.ecology: Hedgehogs can travel a mile a night hunting beetles and slugs. They hibernate through winter, sometimes waking during mild spells to feed.
safeFacts: A hedgehog out in daylight often needs help — contact a wildlife rescue and offer shallow water, not milk.
